paras: The lynching of Wilbur Little was the killing of a Black returned soldier, named in the Black press as Private Wilbur Little or Private Wylie Jr. Little, who was beaten to death by a mob near Blakely, Georgia, shortly before April 4, 1919. According to the only news dispatch on the case, he had been ordered to stop wearing his army uniform and told to leave town, and he was attacked after he refused. Black papers held the case up as an example of the treatment Black soldiers met in the South on their return from the war.

Little was described as a prominent young man of the vicinity and a member of one of the most respectable families in the community. When he arrived home a few weeks before the dispatch was written, he was halted at the station and told to strip off his uniform before he walked down the main thoroughfares of the town. He was threatened with arrest unless he complied, but because he had no civilian clothes he was allowed to go home in uniform. Afterward, the dispatch said, 'a certain white element' advised him to 'take off' the uniform, and several anonymous communications told him to leave town if he wanted to 'sport around in his khaki.'

Little refused, and the dispatch said this refusal of a 'nefarious order cost him his life.' Later, while he stood on the street receiving congratulations from friends, a mob attacked him and beat him to death. In the dispatch's words, 'He was lynched in the uniform.' The report gave no date for the killing beyond 'recently' and named no member of the mob.
No report of an arrest, inquest or trial appears in the coverage.

The story first appeared on the front page of the Chicago Defender on April 5, 1919, as a Century News Service dispatch datelined Blakeley, Ga., April 4, under a headline saying the army uniform had cost him his life and a subhead reading 'Say-At-Homes Object to Presence of Khaki—Mob Acts.' The Defender's text named the victim 'Private Wylie Jr. Little,' while the later printings gave 'Private Wilbur Little.' The Baltimore Afro-American reprinted the dispatch on April 11 under the headline 'Georgia Soldier Lynchd,' credited it to The Defender, and printed the dateline as 'Bleicher, Ga., April 19.' The Colorado Statesman ran the full text on its front page the next day.

In an editorial in the same April 11 issue, the Afro-American pointed readers to 'the lynching of a colored soldier in GEORGIA because he kept his uniform on too long' as one of the 'bits of every day news from Southern states.' The Cleveland Gazette returned to the case on June 7 in a sarcastic editorial, 'Getting Back to Normal,' which placed it at Blakely and described 'An Afro-American soldier, just back from France,' who was 'too slow in complying' with an order to stop wearing his uniform. A Savannah Tribune editorial of May 17 on Georgia lynchings and on returned soldiers driven from their homes listed 'Blakley' among the towns marked by mob killings, without naming a victim.

The printings differ on the victim's first name, 'Wylie Jr.' in the Defender and 'Wilbur' in the Afro-American and the Colorado Statesman, and on the town, given as 'Blakeley,' 'Blakely' and 'Bleicher.' Because the Afro-American's text is the same dispatch and its 'April 19' dateline falls after its own April 11 issue date, 'Bleicher' is most likely a misprint for Blakeley.

reader.title: Lynching of Wilbur Little
bases: A mob beat a returned Black soldier to death after he refused orders to remove his army uniform and leave town (A3, A7, A9).

The dispatch says a mob beat Little to death and that he 'was lynched in the uniform' (A7, A6); the stated pretext was his refusal to obey an order from 'a certain white element' to stop wearing the uniform, a racial-deference pretext (A7, A4, A9).

All news texts reproduce one Century News Service dispatch (A3, A5, A6, A7; the Afro-American credits The Defender), and the editorials in A4 and A9 comment on it without independent detail beyond A9's 'just back from France'.

accounts.label: Century News Service dispatch (Black press)
accounts.gist: Little, home from the army, was ordered to take off his uniform and told by anonymous letters to leave town; he refused and was later beaten to death by a mob on the street.

accounts.label: Cleveland Gazette editorial
accounts.gist: An Afro-American soldier just back from France, ordered by 'local sentiment' to quit wearing his uniform, was too slow to comply and was lynched at Blakely.

framing.detail: The dispatch called the order 'nefarious' and headlined that the army uniform cost him his life, with the subhead 'Stay-at-Homes Object to Presence of Khaki—Mob Acts'.
The Afro-American headlined 'Georgia Soldier Lynchd' and its editorial cited the case among 'bits of every day news from Southern states'.
The Cleveland Gazette treated it with sarcasm as the South 'getting back to normal' after the war.

conflicts.note: Same dispatch; the Defender's OCR text is heavily garbled, so either form may be a misprint.
'Bleicher' appears only in the Afro-American reprint, whose dateline 'April 19' postdates its own April 11 issue; it is likely a misprint of Blakeley.
